title: Rolling Deployments and Rollback
description: Deploy new application versions with zero downtime using rolling updates, and recover quickly from bad releases using Kubernetes rollback mechanisms.

data.text: A **rolling update** is Kubernetes's default strategy for updating Pods in a Deployment. Instead of taking down all old Pods and then starting new ones (which causes downtime), Kubernetes gradually replaces old Pods with new ones. At every moment during the update, some Pods are still serving the old version while others run the new version. Users experience no interruption.

You control the pace of a rolling update with two settings: `maxSurge` (how many extra Pods can run temporarily) and `maxUnavailable` (how many old Pods can be down at once). Tuning these values lets you balance update speed against resource availability.

terms.definition: A Deployment strategy that gradually replaces old Pods with new ones.
The maximum number of Pods that can exceed the desired replica count during an update.
The maximum number of Pods that can be unavailable during an update.
Reverting a Deployment to a previous revision if the new version is faulty.
Each rollout creates a new ReplicaSet; Kubernetes keeps the old ones for rollback.

data.text: When you update the Pod template in a Deployment (e.g., change the container image tag), Kubernetes detects the change and starts a new rollout. It creates a new ReplicaSet with the updated template and gradually scales it up while scaling down the old ReplicaSet. The speed and safety of this process depend on your `strategy` configuration.

data.title: Deployment with rolling update strategy
data.content: Control the pace of updates with maxSurge and maxUnavailable.
data.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: myregistry.io/web:2.3.1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80

data.text: If a new release introduces bugs or performance issues, you can roll back to the previous known-good version with a single command. Kubernetes keeps the history of ReplicaSet revisions, so rollbacks are instant and reliable. You can roll back to any previous revision, not just the immediately preceding one.

data.title: Rolling back a Deployment
data.content: Use kubectl rollout commands to inspect and undo a deployment.
data.code:
# Check rollout history
kubectl rollout history deployment/web-app

# Roll back to the previous revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web-app

# Roll back to a specific revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web-app --to-revision=2

# Watch the rollback progress
kubectl rollout status deployment/web-app

data.title: Rollbacks are fast because ReplicaSets already exist
data.text: Kubernetes does not need to re-pull images during a rollback — it simply scales the old ReplicaSet back up. This makes rollbacks nearly instantaneous, which is why rolling updates + rollbacks are the default for production deployments.

True zero downtime requires more than just rolling updates. Your application must handle being shut down gracefully and must be ready to accept traffic immediately after starting. Here are the key requirements.

items: Container image tag is explicit (not :latest) so Kubernetes detects changes.
Readiness probe is configured so Kubernetes only routes traffic to ready Pods.
Application handles SIGTERM and stops accepting new connections gracefully.
Rolling update strategy has sensible maxSurge and maxUnavailable values.
Database schema changes are backward-compatible (blue-green compatible).
Health endpoints are exposed on a dedicated port or path.

data.title: Perform a rolling update and rollback
data.description: Update an application version and practice rolling back.
steps: Deploy an application with image tag v1.0.0 and 4 replicas.
Update the Deployment to image tag v2.0.0.
Watch the rollout with kubectl rollout status.
While the rollout is in progress, describe a Pod to see the old container being terminated and the new one starting.
Verify all Pods are running v2.0.0 with kubectl get pods.
Simulate a bad release by deploying a non-existent image tag.
Roll back using kubectl rollout undo and verify the version reverted.
data.expectedOutcome: You can perform rolling updates safely and recover quickly from bad deployments using rollbacks.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Rolling updates gradually replace old Pods with new ones, maintaining availability throughout.
maxSurge and maxUnavailable control the speed and safety of each rollout.
Readiness probes ensure traffic only routes to fully started Pods.
Rollbacks are instant because Kubernetes retains old ReplicaSets.
Zero-downtime deployments require readiness probes, graceful shutdown, and backward-compatible changes.
data.takeaway: Rolling updates give you safe, incremental deployments, and rollbacks give you a safety net when things go wrong.
